The card lists G3, G5 as added and G4, G5 as removed, in the same colors." width="100%"} Edges are compared by node labels. The calling graph is treated as the "before" state and `other=` as the "after" state. Each graph is reduced to a set of `(source_label, target_label)` pairs (an unlabelled node is represented by its ID as a string), and the two set differences are returned: edges that appear only in `other=` are reported as added, and edges that appear only in the calling graph are reported as removed. Edges present in both graphs are not listed. This is useful for: - differential network analysis, e.g., interactions gained or lost between a healthy and a disease condition - seeing exactly which edges changed between two versions or snapshots of a network - auditing what a filtering or thresholding step removed Matching follows the same rules as `edge_overlap()`. In undirected graphs `A--B` and `B--A` are the same edge and each tuple is reported with its two labels in sorted order; in directed graphs the tuple keeps the edge direction. Edge weights and attributes are ignored, so an edge whose weight changed is not reported. The order of the tuples within each list is not guaranteed; sort them if you need a stable order. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to compare against, treated as the "after" state. Its edges are matched to this graph's edges by the labels of their endpoints. It should normally have the same directedness as the calling graph. Swapping the two graphs swaps the `added` and `removed` lists. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary with keys: `added` (edges in `other` but not in `self`) and `removed` (edges in `self` but not in `other`). Each value is a list of `(source_label, target_label)` tuples, which is empty if there is nothing to report. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_overlap`) : Summarize the shared and unique edges as counts and a Jaccard index. [](`~graph_edit_distance`) : Also count node insertions and deletions. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A five-gene network in two conditions. In the second condition the interaction between `G4` and `G5` is lost and a new one between `G3` and `G5` appears, so each list holds a single edge. Note that the new edge was added as `G5`, `G3` but is reported in sorted order as `("G3", "G5")`: ::: {#4a887143 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec genes = ["G1", "G2", "G3", "G4", "G5"] ring = [("G1", "G2"), ("G2", "G3"), ("G3", "G4"), ("G4", "G5"), ("G5", "G1"), ("G1", "G3")] healthy = ec.Graph() healthy.add_nodes(genes) healthy.add_edges(ring) disease = ec.Graph() disease.add_nodes(genes) disease.add_edges([(s, t) for s, t in ring if (s, t) != ("G4", "G5")]) disease.add_edge("G5", "G3") healthy.differential_edges(disease) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'added': [('G3', 'G5')], 'removed': [('G4', 'G5')]} ``` ::: ::: Reversing the comparison swaps the roles of the two lists: ::: {#742de70f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} disease.differential_edges(healthy) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'added': [('G4', 'G5')], 'removed': [('G3', 'G5')]} ``` ::: :::
